messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Cross validation with Lavaan
parts:
I'm not sure I follow the logic of what you are doing, but you say you have been able to do it in Mplus by saving parameter estimates as starting values with the SVALUE command (presumably changing each asterisk * to @ so they become constraints instead of starting values).  If this is the only thing you need to know how to do, then something like the following should work (although you should check the "C.syntax" to make sure it contains all the constraints you expect):

example(sem) ## just to get an example to work with
E.coefs <- parameterEstimates(fit)
E.coefs
C.syntax <- paste0(E.coefs$lhs, E.coefs$op, E.coefs$est, "*", E.coefs$rhs, collapse = "\n")
cat(C.syntax) ## this should be the syntax of constraints you need

There might be something easier or more clever that I am unaware of.

Terry

Used on the other half of the sample, the degree of misfit should give you an indication of the stability of your model.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Cross validation with Lavaan
parts:
The cross-validation methods Franck and Ross have described sound more appropriate for regression models than for SEM.  Because factor scores are unobserved and indeterminate, they are estimated essentially by reversing the roles of predictor and outcome.  That is, the parameters are estimated for a model in which the observed indicators are treated as outcomes, with latent factors as predictors.  Then predicted values of factor scores are estimated by treating them as outcomes in an equation where the observed indicators are predictors.  I would not suggest using factor score estimates as though they were observed data because they are arbitrary, not actually factor scores.  Ed Rigdon has posted much on this topic elsewhere on the lavaan boards and on SEMNET (for example: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/gPdwR7jtQYo/ejke5wBt_GUJ )

To calculate an actual cross-validation index, you don't need to estimate factor scores at all.  You simply need to estimate the model parameters on the calibration data (which Franck called E), extract the model-implied covariance matrix (Sigma_E), and compare Sigma_E to the observed covariance matrix of the validation data (which Franck called C above).  You can use the same ML fit function equation that is used to calculate the discrepancy between the model-implied and observed covariance matrices in the results for E, and the chi-squared value is simply N times that fit function:

http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/discrep.html

If you have a non-saturated mean structure, you also need to add a term to the fit function that takes into account the observed (M) and model-implied (mu) mean vectors: (M - mu) %*% Sigma-inverse %*% (M - mu)

This discrepancy measure is called the cross-validation index (CVI), and you can see a discussion of it on pp. 241-242 of this article:

http://smr.sagepub.com/content/21/2/230.abstract

They introduce CVI before discussing the expected CVI (the ECVI is available in lavaan using the fitMeasures() function), which can be calculated if you don't have enough data for a separate hold-out sample -- but it is linearly equivalent to AIC.  But since you have separate samples, you can calculate an actual CVI, and I imagine you can interpret it by multiplying it by N to put it on a chi-squared metric (using the same degrees of freedom).

Terry
